original_question: How should quantum theory account for the arrow of time in cosmology: through a genuine collapse law or through Everettian branching plus decoherence, and what initial condition is needed in either case? In particular, if a non-unitary collapse law has never been experimentally confirmed and Everett branching remains a live alternative, how is the time arrow of decoherence to be grounded in the initial global wave function so that recoherence is suppressed and quasi-classical worlds arise with a definite temporal orientation?
target_in_paper: Section 3, page P8, lines 195–202, where Zeh states: “While the collapse would define a time-asymmetric law, the time arrow of decoherence (formation of retarded entanglement) must again arise as a consequence of an initial condition – now for the global wave function. A universally valid Schrödinger equation would in principle also admit the anti-causal process of recoherence, but this is very rare under an appropriate initial condition...”
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies that Zeh contrasts a genuine collapse law (never experimentally confirmed) with Everettian branching via decoherence, and that in the unitary case the time arrow of decoherence must be grounded in a special initial global wave function that suppresses recoherence and yields quasi-classical branches with definite temporal orientation.
missing_details: Specification that the initial state must be non-entangled (a “simple” symmetric state) in order to evolve into asymmetric Everett branches under a symmetric Hamiltonian
Clarification that the global wave function obeys a universally valid Schrödinger equation (e.g., Wheeler–DeWitt equation for Friedmann universes)
Definition of “retarded entanglement” as the decoherence mechanism specifying autonomous branches
Quantitative description of what counts as a “very rare” recoherence under the chosen initial condition
Explicit scope restriction to cosmological models with a global quantum state rather than laboratory systems
refined_question: In the framework of a universally valid Schrödinger evolution for the global wave function of the universe (as, for example, in the Wheeler–DeWitt approach for Friedmann cosmologies), should the observed cosmological arrow of time be implemented by (a) a fundamentally time-asymmetric non-unitary collapse law—despite the lack of experimental confirmation for any modification of the Schrödinger equation—or by (b) Everettian branching defined by irreversible decoherence (retarded entanglement) under unitary evolution? Specifically, what precise initial condition on the global wave function (e.g., a non-entangled “simple” symmetric state) is required to suppress recoherence to a negligible probability and thereby guarantee the emergence of autonomous quasi-classical branches with a well-defined temporal orientation?
justification: This question is formulated to match Zeh’s open problem exactly: he contrasts collapse and Everett branches (P7, L190–194) and emphasizes that in the unitary case the time arrow of decoherence itself must stem from a special initial global wave function that prevents recoherence (P8, L195–202).
